prompt.context: You are a Bain Consultant. In 30 minutes you are scheduled to meet with a Bain Partner and the CEO of a $35B pharma client — Bolsen — to present a project update. However, the CEO just called saying he would like to change the topic of the meeting and asked the Partner one question: should the company enter the oncology (cancer) market? The CEO is eager to hear your ideas in 30 minutes. You need to discuss with the Partner and prepare a recommendation.
prompt.question: Should Bolsen Pharma enter the oncology (cancer) market? If so, how?

clarifying_info.q: What are Bolsen's current products and competitive position?
clarifying_info.a: Bolsen has mature products, high capitalization, but little growth, and confronts increased competition from generic drug manufacturers driving down prices.

clarifying_info.q: What growth target would make entry worthwhile?
clarifying_info.a: Bolsen will enter the oncology market only if that new market can help Bolsen gain double-digit growth on its overall business.

clarifying_info.q: What R&D capabilities does Bolsen currently have?
clarifying_info.a: Bolsen currently has very basic R&D capability far below the required R&D level for oncology products.

clarifying_info.q: What geographies is Bolsen concerned with?
clarifying_info.a: Bolsen operates in the US and is only concerned about the US market.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape in oncology?
clarifying_info.a: The market is concentrated. A strong player like Genentech has 5 great products and takes 35% market share. Basis of competition is product and technology.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any M&A targets available?
clarifying_info.a: All strong market players including Genentech have been acquired by large Pharma, except for Selgen in New Jersey. Selgen has 2 great products and 10% market share.

clarifying_info.q: Does Bolsen have the financial resources to make an acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Bolsen has a lot of cash and access to capital markets.

framework: Oncology Market Assessment: size, growth rate, and attractiveness
Competition: share concentration, basis of competition, and what it takes to compete
Method of Market Entry: build vs. buy — note Bolsen's R&D capability gap vs. oncology requirements points to M&A
M&A Target Screening: identify viable targets and assess strategic fit
Client Capability: financing capability, M&A experience, post-merger integration readiness

questions.prompt: Estimate the size of the US oncology (cancer) drug market.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up from population data. Strong answer walks through deaths per year, cancer share, patients living with cancer at any time, treatments per year, and revenue per treatment. Conclusion: market is large (~$36B) and attractive. If Bolsen captures 10% that equals $3–4B in revenue, enough to meet the double-digit growth target on a $35B base.

math.setup: Use US population 320M and life expectancy 80 years to estimate annual deaths, then layer in cancer's share, patient duration, treatment frequency, and cost per treatment.
steps: Deaths per year due to cancer = 4M × 25% = 1M
Patients living with cancer at any time = 1M × 5 years = 5M
Treatments per year = 5M × (2 treatments / 5 years) = 2M treatments

questions.prompt: What is the growth outlook for the oncology market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify demand-side growth drivers rather than just assert 'it is growing.' Strong answer covers: patients living longer due to treatments pushing up patient count, more frequent treatments as medicine advances, higher willingness to pay / higher drug prices, earlier cancer diagnoses catching more patients. Conclusion: high growth rate — in reality over 20%.

questions.prompt: Given Bolsen's R&D capability gap, how should Bolsen enter the oncology market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should explicitly recognize that Bolsen cannot compete by building internal R&D — capability is far below oncology requirements. This should lead the candidate to recommend M&A as the entry route. Strong answer then screens M&A targets: need a player with enough products to reach 10%+ market share. Genentech benchmark: 5 products → 35% share ≈ 7% per great product. Therefore Bolsen needs a target with at least 2 great products. Selgen (2 products, 10% share, still independent) is the ideal target. Bolsen has cash and capital market access to finance the deal.

math.setup: Use Genentech's market share as a benchmark to estimate share per great product, then determine how many products Bolsen needs to hit 10% share.
steps: Genentech: 35% share / 5 great products = 7% share per great product
Target: need ≥10% share → need at least 2 great products (2 × 7% ≈ 14%)
Selgen has 2 great products and already holds 10% share — meets the threshold
math.answer: Selgen is the ideal acquisition target: 2 products, 10% market share, last major independent player.

questions.prompt: All large pharma companies have gone through the same logic. Why haven't they already acquired Selgen?
questions.guidance: This is a push-back / stress-test question. Candidate should brainstorm possible reasons the market has not cleared. Strong answers cover several of the following: Selgen does not want to sell; Selgen's key R&D talent has already left; Selgen's patents will expire soon making the asset less valuable; Selgen is asking for an unreasonably high price (actual answer: they demand a 20× multiple vs. a normal 10× multiple).

brainstorming.prompt: Why might large pharma companies have not yet acquired Selgen despite it being an obvious target?

categories.name: Seller-side unwillingness
ideas: Selgen does not want to sell itself

categories.name: Asset quality concerns
ideas: Selgen's key R&D people have already left the company
Selgen's patents will expire soon, reducing future value

categories.name: Price / deal structure
ideas: Selgen is asking for a very high price (20× revenue multiple vs. normal 10×)
Deal terms are unattractive to acquirers

recommendation: Bolsen should acquire Selgen to enter the oncology market

Rationale: $36B market with high growth rate (>20%); Bolsen lacks R&D capability but has ample cash; Selgen (2 products, 10% share) is the last available independent target; acquisition would give Bolsen the double-digit revenue growth it requires
risks: Selgen may demand a very high acquisition price (20× multiple vs. normal 10×)
Post-merger integration challenges (culture, talent retention, R&D continuity)
Bolsen's limited M&A experience may create execution risk
next_steps: Conduct full due diligence on Selgen (pipeline, patents, talent, financials)
Find ways to boost Selgen's revenue by ~100% as quickly as possible so the effective acquisition multiple returns to ~10×
Ensure Bolsen's leadership is fully committed to the oncology market — prior large pharma acquisitions with poor focus led to poor results
